Changing the key: tuned-down recordings, capo, and vocal range

Loop Trainer can move a recording up or down by up to 6 semitones without changing its tempo. This is useful whenever the recording and your instrument (or your voice) are not in the same key.

Semitones in one minute

A semitone (half step) is the distance of one fret on a guitar. Twelve semitones make an octave. Shifting the key by +1 raises every note by one fret's worth: E becomes F, A becomes B♭. Each semitone changes the pitch by a factor of 1.0595, so +2 is 1.122 times the original frequency.

Changing the key on a record player or a tape changes the speed too. Loop Trainer changes the pitch and the speed separately, so you can use the key and the speed together: for example −1 and 70%.

How many semitones? Common situations

SituationKey setting
The recording is tuned down a half step (E♭ tuning), and you play in standard tuning+1
The recording is tuned down a whole step (D tuning), and you play in standard tuning+2
The recording is in standard tuning, and your guitar is tuned down a half step−1
The recording uses a capo on fret 2, and you want to play the same shapes without a capo−2
The recording uses a capo on fret 3, and you want to put your capo on fret 1−2
The song is too high to sing−1 to −3, as far as it feels comfortable

The rule behind all of these: move the recording toward where your instrument is. If the recording is lower than your guitar, shift it up; if it is higher, shift it down.

Many rock and metal recordings are in E♭ tuning. If the chords you hear seem to sit between two frets, try +1 first.

Tips

  • Small shifts sound most natural. One or two semitones are hard to notice; larger shifts make voices sound a little unnatural.
  • Check by ear. Play a note along with the recording. If it beats or sounds sour, try one semitone either way.
  • The key is saved for each song, together with the loops and the speed. “Original key” sets it back to ±0.
  • For learning by ear, find the notes in the shifted key, then remember the shift when you write them down. See learning by ear.
